01

Cycles

Water and carbon move through the Earth system on very different clocks.

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B02 / 40

The water cycle

Movement and phase change

The processes

Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff — and the phase changes that move energy with the water.

The reservoirs

Oceans, ice, groundwater, soil moisture, rivers, and the atmosphere. Each holds water for a characteristic length of time.

Phase change is how the water cycle transports energy, not just mass. That coupling is what makes the atmosphere hard to model.

Processes driving movement and phase change in water

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B03 / 40

The water cycle

Where humans enter the loop

Withdrawals

Irrigation, industry and public supply move water out of one reservoir and into another.

Land surface

Reservoirs, drainage and urban surfaces change how much water runs off and how fast.

The natural cycle and the managed one are now the same cycle. Fluxes on this diagram are annual averages, which conceal a great deal of local variation.

Human impact on the water cycle

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B04 / 40

Where the water goes

Precipitation minus evaporation

The equator

Dominated by precipitation — more water falls than leaves.

The subtropics

Dominated by evaporation — the source regions for atmospheric moisture.

The banded pattern is a consequence of large-scale circulation, not of where the land happens to be. Any model that gets this map wrong has a circulation problem.

Yearly average precipitation minus evaporation

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B05 / 40

Quiz · water cycle

Residence time

Q1Which reservoir holds water the longest on average — rivers, oceans, glaciers, or Antarctica?
Q2And which holds it for the shortest time — atmosphere, soil moisture, seasonal snow, or lakes?
Vote, then reveal

Commit to both answers before the reveal.

Longest: Antarctica — ice there can be locked up for tens of thousands of years, longer than the ocean’s average. Shortest: the atmosphere, where the average residence time is on the order of days. That short atmospheric residence time is exactly why weather changes so fast.
AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B06 / 40

Ocean circulation

The thermohaline conveyor

What drives it

Density gradients set up by surface heating and freshwater fluxes. Cold, salty water sinks; warmer water flows in to replace it.

Why it matters

It redistributes heat between hemispheres on a timescale of centuries — far slower than anything in a weather forecast.

Deep-water formation happens in a few small regions. A circulation that spans the planet is controlled at a handful of places.

The global conveyor belt — surface and deep currents

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B07 / 40

ENSO · the normal state

Quasi-equilibrium and La Niña

In the west

Equatorial winds gather a warm water pool toward the western Pacific, where it drives deep atmospheric convection.

In the east

Local winds cause nutrient-rich cold water to upwell at the equator and along the South American coast.

The upwelling is not incidental — it is the base of a fishery. An ocean-atmosphere oscillation is also an economy.

Normal conditions and the La Niña phase

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B08 / 40

ENSO · the warm phase

El Niño

The warm pool moves east

It approaches the South American coast, and atmospheric convection moves with it.

Upwelling fails

A deeper thermocline means the water that does upwell is warm and nutrient-poor. The absence of cold upwelling reinforces the warming.

Note the feedback: the warming suppresses the process that would have cooled it. Self-reinforcing loops are why the system flips between states rather than drifting smoothly.

The El Niño phase of the Southern Oscillation

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B09 / 40

Quiz · El Niño and La Niña

Which one does not belong?

Q1Which is NOT associated with El Niño?
Q2Which is NOT associated with La Niña?
Discuss in pairs, then reveal

Work from the mechanism rather than from memory: where is the warm pool, and which way does convection move?

Q1 — flooding in the Pacific Northwest. El Niño shifts the jet stream southward, tending to leave the Pacific Northwest drier rather than flooded. Q2 — dry weather in the Pacific Northwest. La Niña tends to bring the opposite. The two questions are mirror images, which is the point: name the mechanism and both answers follow.
AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B10 / 40

The carbon cycle

A slower loop, with a leak

Fast exchange

Photosynthesis and respiration move carbon between atmosphere, plants and soils every year.

Ocean uptake

The surface ocean absorbs a net share of emissions, with the deep ocean holding by far the largest stock.

The imbalance

Fossil fuels and land use add carbon that the fast loops do not return, so the atmospheric stock rises each year.

Water goes up and comes back down. Human-produced carbon dioxide largely goes up and stays — that asymmetry is the whole problem in one sentence.

The carbon cycle — stocks and annual fluxes

02

Climate change

What it means, what the data say, and what follows from it.

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B12 / 40

Greenhouse gases

Which gases, and why water is different

Carbon dioxide

The dominant human-added gas, and the longest-lived of the main ones.

Methane

Shorter-lived, but far more effective per molecule while it lasts.

Nitrous oxide

Largely from agriculture and industry.

Water vapour

The largest greenhouse gas by effect — but held in a tight cycle: what goes up comes back down.

Water vapour responds to temperature rather than setting it, which is why it is treated as a feedback rather than a driver. Human emissions of the others accumulate.

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B13 / 40

The mechanism

Why a greenhouse warms

The analogy

A car on a cool but sunny day: sunlight passes in through the glass, the interior warms, and the heat does not leave as easily as it arrived.

In Earth terms

Sunlight enters the atmosphere. Some heat is absorbed, some reflected. Most of the rest should radiate back to space — greenhouse gases keep part of it in the atmosphere.

The analogy is useful and imperfect: a car is warm mainly because the air cannot circulate out, while the atmosphere is warm because of how gases absorb and re-emit radiation.

Incoming sunlight, outgoing heat, and what the atmosphere retains

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B14 / 40

The evidence

What is already measurable

Converging lines

Combined land and ocean temperature, Arctic sea-ice extent, global mean sea level, and precipitation over land — measured by different instruments, by different people.

Why decadal averages

Averaging over a decade removes much of the year-to-year noise. On the decadal panel the recent boxes no longer overlap the earlier ones.

Precipitation is the most spatially variable of the four: some regions have become considerably wetter while others have become drier, which a global average hides entirely.

Observed changes in temperature, sea ice, sea level and precipitation

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B15 / 40

Causes

Natural and human drivers

Natural

  • Volcanic eruptions
  • Plate tectonics moving landmasses
  • Changes in solar output
  • Shifts in Earth’s orbit

Human

  • Burning fossil fuels
  • Burning forests and grasslands
  • Industrial processes
  • Agriculture

Natural climate variability is real and has always happened — which is not an argument against human-caused change, because the natural drivers operate on very different timescales. Orbital shifts take tens to hundreds of thousands of years. A change measured over 150 years needs a cause that can act over 150 years.

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B16 / 40

Emissions

Rising, and accelerating

The trend

Annual emissions of every major greenhouse gas rose across the period, with carbon dioxide from fossil fuels and industry dominating the total.

The detail worth noticing

The increase in the first decade of this century exceeded the increase over the three decades before it.

“CO₂ FOLU” on this figure means forestry and other land use — a separate bar from fossil fuels and industry.

Total annual anthropogenic greenhouse-gas emissions by gas

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B17 / 40

Attribution

What the IPCC concluded

The findingHuman-caused greenhouse gases, together with other anthropogenic drivers, have been detected throughout the climate system and are extremely likely to have been the dominant cause of observed warming since the mid-20th century.
Who says soThe Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change — hundreds of scientists synthesising thousands of studies, reviewed by other scientists and by governments.
On the wording“Extremely likely” is a defined confidence term, not a rhetorical flourish. The vocabulary is part of the method.

Reports of this kind take years to assemble precisely because of that review process — which is also why any single new paper rarely overturns one.

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B18 / 40

Projected effects

What follows, and for how long

Momentum

Warming and sea-level rise continue for centuries even if greenhouse gases are stabilised. Some effects, such as lost glaciers, may be effectively permanent.

Ecosystems

Coral systems handle higher temperatures poorly, wildfire risk increases, and a substantial share of species faces heightened extinction risk.

North America

Less mountain snowpack, more winter flooding and less summer water; longer and more intense heat waves; coastal flooding and storms.

Note who bears these costs. Coastal adaptation is a budgeting question in a wealthy country and a displacement question in a poor one.

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B19 / 40

Closer to home

New York and lake-effect snow

The mechanism

Cold air crosses relatively warm lake water, picks up heat and moisture, and dumps it as narrow, intense snow bands downwind.

The twist

Warmer lakes that freeze later can mean more lake-effect snow, not less — until the air itself is too warm for snow.

A good example of why “warmer means less snow” is too simple a rule. The local answer depends on which term in the mechanism changes first.

Lake-effect snow bands downwind of the Great Lakes

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B20 / 40

Mitigation

Emission pathways

What the bands show

Annual emissions under no climate policies, current policies, and pledges — each with an associated warming range by 2100.

What the width means

The spread is uncertainty, and it is wide. Policy choice moves the central line; physical and economic uncertainty sets the band around it.

These are conditional projections, not forecasts. Which band the world is on is a decision, not a measurement.

Global greenhouse-gas emission pathways under different policy assumptions

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B21 / 40

Mitigation

Removing and storing carbon

Capture and store

Separate carbon dioxide at the source or from the air, then inject it into depleted reservoirs, coal beds or deep saline formations.

Biological routes

Soil amendments and carbon-based products hold carbon in the land system instead of the atmosphere.

Ask of any storage proposal: for how long, at what cost per tonne, and at what scale relative to current annual emissions. All three answers matter and the third usually disappoints.

Capture, separation and geological storage

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B22 / 40

Quiz · climate change

Two on sources

Q1What has contributed most to carbon dioxide emissions since 1880 — land use, coal, oil, or gas?
Q2Which food has the highest supply-chain greenhouse-gas emissions — beef, lamb, cheese, or chocolate?
Vote, then reveal

Commit before the reveal — and for Q2, say which unit you are comparing in.

Q1: coal. Q2: beef from a beef herd, by a wide margin per kilogram. The unit matters — per kilogram, per gram of protein and per calorie give different orderings, and any of the three can be the fair comparison depending on the question you are asking.

03

Maps

How the atmosphere is made visible — and how a map hides its own assumptions.

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B24 / 40

Weather maps

From national forecast to local sensor

The national view

A forecast map covers the country at a resolution that suits a regional decision, and no finer.

The mesonet

A dense network of local stations measures what actually fell, station by station — the ground truth a forecast is scored against.

New York’s mesonet exists because a state-wide forecast cannot resolve a thunderstorm over one county. Resolution is a choice about which decisions you intend to support.

Mesonet 24-hour rainfall accumulation

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B25 / 40

Observing maps

Satellite and radar see different things

Satellite

Measures radiation from cloud tops and the surface. Excellent coverage; tells you about the top of the atmosphere more than the bottom.

Radar

Sends a pulse and listens for what bounces back off precipitation. Tells you where rain is falling, and estimates how hard — indirectly.

Neither instrument measures rainfall directly at the ground. Both produce an estimate that a rain gauge can contradict.

Satellite view over the northeastern United States

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B26 / 40

Maps of motion and of extremes

Wind fields and event catalogues

Wind flow

Vectors show direction and speed across a grid — the same field a numerical model advances forward in time.

Extreme events

A dot map of recorded events is partly a map of where instruments and reporting exist.

This is the observation-bias point again, in cartographic form. Sparse regions on an event map may be sparsely affected, sparsely measured, or sparsely reported — and the map cannot tell you which.

Global map of recorded extreme events

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B27 / 40

Climate maps

From short-term to long-term

What it shows

A Köppen map classifies places by the distribution of their weather — humid subtropical, oceanic, humid continental.

What it is built from

Thirty-year climate normals. A single unusual year cannot move a boundary; a sustained shift can.

A weather map is a snapshot of the state. A climate map is a picture of the distribution. Same atmosphere, different object.

Köppen climate types of New York State

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B28 / 40

When the map moves

Plant hardiness zones, 2012 and 2023

What the map encodes

The average annual extreme minimum temperature — the coldest night a typical year delivers. It tells a grower what will survive the winter.

What changed

Between the 2012 and 2023 editions, zone boundaries shifted northward across much of the country.

Read this carefully: a zone revision reflects updated normals and methodology as well as warming, so it is evidence to interpret rather than a thermometer. It is also the version of climate change a farmer actually has to plan around.

2023 USDA plant hardiness zone map

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B29 / 40
04

Modelling the atmosphere

Equations on a grid — and the reasons that is harder than it sounds.

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B30 / 40

The system

What a model has to represent

The exchanges

Radiation from the sun and from the Earth, evaporation and heat exchange at the surface, cloud formation, terrain effects, friction.

The coupling

None of these is independent. Change the cloud cover and you change the radiation, which changes the evaporation, which changes the cloud cover.

Coupled feedbacks are why you cannot model one process well in isolation and expect the whole to be right.

Radiation, evaporation, orography and cloud formation

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B31 / 40

How NWP works

Observations in, forecast out

Observe

Surface, balloon, satellite and radar data.

Initialise

Build the model’s starting state.

Integrate

Run the physical equations forward.

Forecast

Read out the future state.

Each grid cell exchanges heat, moisture and momentum with its neighbours, horizontally and vertically, at every time step.

Everything smaller than a grid cell — an individual cloud, a thunderstorm updraught — has to be represented by an approximation rather than simulated.

Block diagram for numerical weather prediction

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B32 / 40

Why it is hard

The butterfly, and what it really claims

The demonstration

Two double pendulums released from almost the same position track each other for a while, then diverge completely. No randomness is involved.

The claim

The exact time and path of a tornado can be influenced by a perturbation as small as a distant butterfly, weeks earlier.

What it does not claim: that forecasting is hopeless. Deterministic detail is lost quickly; the statistics of the system remain predictable, which is why a seasonal outlook can be useful when a day-20 forecast is not.

Identical double pendulums, released almost identically

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B33 / 40

The data

Where the numbers come from

Four instruments

Stations measure at the surface; balloons profile the air above; satellites orbit and observe globally; radar detects precipitation in between.

Open archives

Reanalysis and model archives — ESGF, NASA’s climate data services — are what make training a large model possible at all.

Every AI weather model in the next section is trained on decades of this. The dataset is the product of public observing systems, accumulated over many years by people who were not building an AI model.

Stations, balloons, satellites and radar

05

Deep learning enters

What changed after 2023 — and what the benchmark numbers actually say.

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B35 / 40

Learned forecast models

Three architectures, one idea

Pangu-Weather3-D transformer architecture. Strong short-range accuracy, and orders of magnitude faster than NWP at inference. Bi et al., Nature 2023
FourCastNetAdaptive Fourier neural operators. Very fast inference with accuracy comparable to NWP for some variables.
GraphCastA graph neural network. Beat HRES on more than 90% of 1,380 targets. Lam et al., Science 2023

The shared idea is the same one from Lecture 7A: learn a mapping from recent atmospheric states to later ones, instead of integrating equations forward.

Model specializations and stated strengths

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B36 / 40

Probabilistic forecasting

GenCast, and a correction worth making

What GenCast is

A diffusion-based generative model producing a 15-day ensemble. It beat ECMWF’s ENS on 97.2% of 1,320 targets in the 2019 test. <i>Price et al., Nature 2024</i>

The easy mix-up

GraphCast is the graph network that beat the deterministic HRES; GenCast is the diffusion model that beat the ENS ensemble. Different architectures, different baselines, different claims.

The decision curves matter more than the win rate: a better probabilistic forecast is worth something only where it changes what somebody does about an approaching extreme.

Better forecasts of extreme weather support better decisions

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B37 / 40

Foundation models

Pre-train once, adapt many times

The pitch

Train on broad Earth-observation data, then fine-tune for forecasting, downscaling, or a specific region.

The example

ClimaX was proposed as a unified, flexible model that could be adapted across climate and weather tasks with limited data.

The open question

Whether one pre-trained model genuinely transfers, or whether each task still needs its own carefully built system.

Hype or hope is the honest framing. Judge a foundation-model claim the way you would any other: on a blind benchmark, at the lead times and variables you care about.

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B38 / 40

Applications

Rain, floods, fire, heat

Where it works well

Short-range precipitation, flood extent, and heat — problems with dense observations, frequent events, and a clear target to predict.

Where it strains

Wildfire and rare compound extremes, where events are scarce in the training record and the drivers extend well beyond the atmosphere.

The pattern across all four: the method works best exactly where we already had the most data, which is not always where the need is greatest.

Precipitation prediction against ground truth

AI × Climate Science · Lecture 7B39 / 40

Summary · exit ticket

What AI brought, and what it owes

Advantages

  • Speed — seconds instead of hours
  • Resolution — super-resolution of coarse fields
  • Integration — satellite, radar, ground, sensors together
  • Adaptability — fine-tune for a region or a phenomenon

Challenges

  • Data quality — noisy, missing, biased inputs
  • Generalization — rare and unprecedented events
  • Interpretability — harder to explain than physics
  • Trust — operational use demands validation
Exit ticket · 2 min

Every advantage in the left column depends on something in the right. Pick one pair and write the sentence that links them.

Example: speed depends on data quality. A model that runs in seconds can be re-run hundreds of times — which multiplies the value of a good training archive and the damage from a biased one. Or: adaptability strains generalization, because fine-tuning to a region with few extreme events can make the model confident exactly where its evidence is thinnest.
